And I don’t know, it’s always fun I think to explore onboarding because the ideal version of onboarding, the thing I’ve always tried to do or try to think about is what would it be like to sit next to somebody and walk them through the product?

But before that, it had been a long time. It’d probably been months, maybe in some cases it could even have been a year. There’s always opportunities for these things to drift so that your nice onboarding flow, yeah, it was nice when you designed it and then seven things changed in the product and things moved around and maybe you introduced new features or whatever and you just don’t see it or it just didn’t keep up. You kept evolving the product, you kept making it better and improving and so on. But the signup process is as it was on launch day because that was the last time you looked at it. So I think those are some of the structural factors of why it often seems weird because as a new customer, this is the thing you see. The first thing you see is the onboarding flow.

So you of course assume that it’s going to be the best that that team has to offer. And that’s just not the case. In almost all cases, onboarding flow is going to be substantially worse than the rest of the product if someone had kept working on it because all the attention goes somewhere else. So having gone through that and then having seen it on the inside gives me a little more empathy when I go through one of those kind of mediocre or even shitty onboarding flows where I go like, “Wow, why can’t they just? How could they not see this?” And I go like, “Yeah, maybe I wouldn’t have seen it either.”

And how would they ever know? You can make a marketing site about all this stuff, but people aren’t going to even look at that. They want to watch something. They want to walk through something and it’s fun to show these things off. I think the other thing we try to do with Basecamp 5 onboarding is not only introduce people to the product, but introduce people to us. Like what are we like as a company? Who are we? Which is why you’re heavily featured. Look, we have friendly faces here. We talk in normal words. We don’t use ridiculous technical jargon. Also, the first thing you see when you sign up is a letter from me. Obviously it’s a form letter. I wrote it once. I’m not writing each person a letter, but it’s like, hey, here I am and here’s my email address. Write me if you have any questions.

I don’t think they really know what they want necessarily. And also the products become more and more alike, not more and more different from one another. And then it’s like, why do you exist? Why are there five things that kind of do the same thing? So I think differentiating yourselves not only in terms of the product offering, but also in terms of who you are, how approachable you are, presentable you are, open you are to communication is a fundamentally important thing that we try to do as often as we can. And I think the onboarding process is the first example of that.

Well, you can check out our new onboarding with a new Basecamp account at basecamp.com. Check it out, sign up for an account for free, and you can see that in-app the video that we were talking about. We’re going to wrap it up there. Rework is production at 37signals. You can find show notes and transcripts on our website at 37signals.com/podcast. Full video episodes on YouTube. And if you have a question for Jason or David about a better way to work and run your business, leave us a video. You can do that, 37signals.com/podcastquestion or send us an email to rework@37signals.com.
evidence.speaker: Kimberly

entities.name: 画中画导览 (picture-in-picture)
entities.how_described: 本集说 Basecamp 5 的画中画导览是在角落放一个小视频，由 Kimberly 出镜引导用户在真实项目里点击、留评论，整个流程约三分钟

evidence.quote: Yeah, onboarding is something that’s always been really fun to work on, although Basecamp never really had a great onboarding. It was decent and there’s some things we did to make it better, but it was a little bit like pointing arrows at things and this is where this is and this is where this is and this is how this works. And when we did HEY a number of years ago, we went through a really nice process of sending you basically a bunch of emails and you have to screen them in because that’s the first step in HEY. And so I’m not going to go into all the detail, but it became this interactive thing that you work through the product to get to understand and learn the product. And we never really had that in Basecamp and now we do. So with Basecamp 5, when you sign up, we have a whole new approach and actually it’s very different. We have a picture-in-picture...
evidence.speaker: Jason

evidence.quote: Yeah, I think that we just kind of hit a new high watermark with HEY actually, where we just had a new product. This is one of the beautiful things about making something brand new is you just like, okay, what can we do here that’s interesting and better? And you build it like, this is really good. I’m really, really... remain very, very proud of the HEY onboarding, the whole procedure and how it works. It’s really good. And so now then you’re shifted into a different orbit and you’re like, this is sort of our new bar and we should bring that kind of thinking to Basecamp. And now we have an opportunity to do that with Basecamp 5. With Basecamp 4, we are already in the middle of the product. It just didn’t feel like the time. We did play with onboarding and improved conversion considerably in fact with Basecamp 4’s onboarding in the middle of that product cycle, but we didn’t redo it really in a sense. This was an opportunity with Basecamp 5 since we’re changing so many things to kind of redo it. And so now what we do is we actually walk you through, it’s about a three-minute tour, like a picture-in-picture tour. And Kimberly, of course, is the star of the onboarding process.
evidence.speaker: Jason

entities.name: 引导漂移 (drift)
entities.how_described: 本集说 drift 是引导流程的结构性问题：发布那天做好了，之后产品不断迭代、东西挪了位置，但注册流程还停在发布日的样子，因为团队自己不注册自己的产品

evidence.quote: But before that, it had been a long time. It’d probably been months, maybe in some cases it could even have been a year. There’s always opportunities for these things to drift so that your nice onboarding flow, yeah, it was nice when you designed it and then seven things changed in the product and things moved around and maybe you introduced new features or whatever and you just don’t see it or it just didn’t keep up. You kept evolving the product, you kept making it better and improving and so on. But the signup process is as it was on launch day because that was the last time you looked at it. So I think those are some of the structural factors of why it often seems weird because as a new customer, this is the thing you see. The first thing you see is the onboarding flow.

entities.name: 稀疏状态 (sparse)
entities.how_described: 本集说 sparse 是产品在数据很少时的状态，比如只有一个项目、两个待办列表时产品长什么样，做产品的人自己天天泡在满是数据的账户里看不到这种状态

evidence.quote: I think one of the reasons why this is hard to do really well is that you don’t see it that often. We are not signing up for Basecamp every day because we already have Basecamp and we’re very engrossed in it and we have a lot of data in it. So one thing is the signup flow, you’re putting in your credentials and you’re getting onboarded. But it’s also what does the product look like when it’s sparse? What does it look like when it only has one project, when it only has two to-do lists? Those states, blank slates we used to call that when there was literally nothing and tried to do some stuff around that, but I think structurally why it’s hard for software companies to really get good at it is because there’s not a lot of iterations. Even for us, this required some very dedicated focus.
evidence.speaker: David

entities.name: 创始人主导的公司 (founder-led companies)
entities.how_described: 本集说 founder-led companies 的魔力在于创始人从零开始手动做过每一单销售，更有可能保持和客户之间的双向连接，不像职业 CEO 那样脱离产品

evidence.quote: You say, Kimberly, like, oh, you’re surprised that Jason would do that. I can understand it’s surprised because most company CEOs, certainly the professional ones never do. And that’s why their shit sucks because they’re not actually exposed to it. It reminds me of the McDonald’s CEO. I’m going to take a bite of this tasty product here. And he takes this little nibble and he looks like a total fucking moron, right? Because he looks like someone who despises his own product, who would never in a million years eat a McDonald’s burger. He just takes a tiny little bite of a product. Not a burger, a product. Already there, just in that language, you know it’s all wrong. You know, here’s someone who doesn’t give two fucks about the actual burger, whether it’s tasty or not. And I think this is the magic in large part about founder-led companies, that someone who went from there was nothing here, I literally had to make every sale manually, is way more likely to stay connected to that exchange, reciprocal exchange.

entities.name: 可用性测试 (usability)
entities.how_described: 本集引用 Jakob Nielsen 在 90 年代提出的 usability，指看着客户实际使用你的产品，才能发现那些愚蠢的绊脚点

evidence.quote: You got to go work on the material. You got to go see if the timing is right and what gets the laughs. And sometimes it’s sort of a throwaway comment that kills that night and you go like, “Oh, okay. I didn’t realize that that would be the trigger point.” And I think you have that a lot in software development as well. We worked on, I don’t know how many features for Basecamp 5. There’s probably hundreds of small changes and trying to guess exactly what’s going to land is surprisingly difficult, but you get to see it when you sit down with someone and you experience them using it. Now, the other thing you get to see is just kind of the stupid things they can stumble over. This is all the way back to Jakob Nielsen back in the ‘90s. Usability, watching customers use your product.
